proposal:
VERDICT: I found no credible universal candidate. Below is the strongest substantially different mechanism I can specify exactly, where it provably stops, and one falsifiable next test.

MECHANISM (DFC-d: dual-field degree-d closure; a sound certifier, only conjecturally a decider). Preprocess: split clauses wider than 3 with fresh variables (equisatisfiable, linear in literal count). Representation: for each p in {2,3}, a reduced row-echelon matrix B_p over GF(p). Columns are the M = sum_{i<=d} C(n,i) <= (n+1)^d multilinear monomials of degree <= d. There are at most M rows and entries take <= 2 bits, so the state is <= 4M^2 bits. No rationals, hence no coefficient growth. Init: each clause C gives the row prod_{positive x in C}(1-x) * prod_{negated x in C} x, the indicator of C's falsifying assignment. Operation: for every row r of degree < d and every variable x, insert multilinearize(x*r) using x^2=x, re-reduce, and repeat until rank stops rising. Cost: <= M rounds, <= nM candidates per round, O(M^2) field operations per reduction, so O(n M^4) = O(n^(4d+1)) constant-size operations per closure. Invariant: every row vanishes on every satisfying assignment of the current formula; linear combination, multiplication by a variable and multilinearization all preserve this. Hence 1 in either span implies UNSAT.

Decision wrapper: if the root closure contains 1, output UNSAT. Otherwise, for i=1..n, fix x_i to a value v whose closure (formula plus row x_i - v) lacks 1. With d>=3 a complete assignment reduces every clause row to a constant, so finishing gives a directly verified SAT. If both values give 1 at depth >=1, output UNKNOWN: that prefix has refutation degree at most d+1, and undoing earlier choices would be the old search. At most 2n+1 closures, so runtime is bounded on every input by n and d alone.

WHAT IS NEW. The prior strategies (DP/branch residuals, equal-residual merging, affine-projection keys) were always correct, with state counts depending on order and cuts and no all-input bound. DFC inverts this. It has no order, cut, residual set or cache, only one fixed-dimension linear space per field. Cost is bounded on all inputs and all uncertainty moves to completeness (UNKNOWN).

CONCEPTUAL TESTS.
(1) XOR: pass. The 2^(k-1) clause rows of a k-XOR are the indicators of its forbidden points, so their GF(2) span contains the linear form. At d>=k DFC contains Gaussian elimination: it refutes inconsistent systems and the wrapper never errs on consistent ones. Neon's 4/8/16 circulant growth disappears.
(2) Mod 3: partial. By the same argument, sum x_i = r (mod 3) becomes a GF(3)-linear row at d>=k, so GF(3)-linearly inconsistent systems are refuted without branching. But x+y+z = 1 (mod 3) on Booleans is exactly-one-in-three SAT, which is NP-complete. Instances that are GF(3)-consistent yet Boolean-UNSAT rely only on multilinearization, with no degree bound.
(3) Pigeonhole: fail. Razborov (1998) gives degree >= n/2 over every field for the standard encoding.
(4) Connected non-affine CNF: fail. Random 3-CNF above threshold needs degree Omega(n) over every field (Ben-Sasson-Impagliazzo; Alekhnovich-Razborov). Tseitin on 3-regular expanders needs Omega(n) over GF(3), though GF(2) wins at d=3. Cost becomes n^(Omega(n)), worse than branching.

NEXT TEST (hypothesis H, not a breakthrough claim). Let D(F) be the least d at which either field derives 1 at root. Generate exactly-one-in-three systems on n=12,15,18,21,24 variables that are GF(3)-linearly consistent but Boolean-UNSAT (brute-force checked). H: max D grows with n, exceeding 3 by n=18 and reaching >=5 by n=24. H is falsified if D<=3 on >=200 instances per size. As an implementation check, run DFC-k (k = constraint width) on Neon's 78-clause fixture: if its constraints are GF(3)-linearly inconsistent, the root must yield 1 over GF(3).
missing_theorem:
First unsupported claim C1: there is a constant d such that every unsatisfiable 3-CNF has 1 in the degree-d closure over GF(2) or GF(3). Equivalently, DFC-d never outputs UNKNOWN. C1 is not merely unproved. It is refuted by published degree lower bounds: random 3-CNF needs Omega(n) over every field, which also rules out d=O(log n) and any d=o(n). So no missing theorem rescues DFC as stated.

Two repairs exist, and I do not propose either.
(a) Add an ordered-ring component (cutting planes, Sherali-Adams, sum-of-squares) to handle pigeonhole. This introduces rational coefficients whose bit lengths need a separate bound. As I recall, random 3-CNF/3-XOR still force linear degree or exponential size there (Grigoriev; Schoenebeck; Hrubes-Pudlak; Fleming et al.).
(b) Add extension variables (extended polynomial calculus). No lower bounds are known, but the closure is no longer finite. Choosing polynomially many extensions that work on all inputs is exactly the missing theorem, and it is a renamed P=NP statement, which the brief excludes.

Non-automatability results (Atserias-Muller for resolution; later work for polynomial calculus and Sherali-Adams, from memory) indicate that even finding short proofs when they exist is NP-hard for these weak systems.

The only statement worth testing is H. It concerns where the degree gap appears on small mod-3 Boolean instances. That bears on DFC's value as a bounded-cost prefilter supplying the parity and mod-3 extraction the current implementation lacks, not on polynomial-time SAT.
self_attack:
1. Nothing here was executed. The indicator/span arguments for XOR and mod 3 are short and I checked them by hand. The O(nM^4) bound is crude but safe. The lower-bound citations are from memory and must be checked against the papers before anyone relies on constants.
2. Razborov's pigeonhole bound concerns the standard wide-clause encoding. I have not verified that it transfers to the split 3-CNF version DFC actually sees. The refutation of C1 does not depend on this, because random 3-CNF and Tseitin are natively width 3.
3. These are theorems about this proof system, not about SAT. They kill DFC as a universal decider and say nothing on P vs NP.
4. Small-n trap: at d=n the closure is complete (all multilinear functions vanishing on the solution set), so at 12 variables a moderate d may succeed trivially. H must be read as growth of D with n. The thresholds 'above 3 by 18, >=5 by 24' are low-confidence guesses. The asymptotic bounds need expansion, which instances this small may lack, so H could fail for that reason alone without making DFC universal.
5. H may be hard to instantiate if GF(3)-consistent, Boolean-UNSAT exactly-one systems are rare at n=12. In that case use mixed residues r in {0,1,2}.
6. UNKNOWN is a real output, and a procedure that can say UNKNOWN is not a SAT algorithm. Hybridising DFC with SCC-E-MRA branching would be a dispatcher, which you excluded.
7. The fixture is null deliberately. The last hand-predicted peak was wrong (actual 1), Canon defeats raw resolvent counting, and zero-reduction DP steps are accepted. Without execution I cannot justify a predicted_peak above 1 for any 12-variable formula, and a guessed fixture would only add noise.
8. The source-watcher handoff was treated as untrusted evidence only. By its own account it holds finite circuit lemmas, a retired lemma and unexplained CI failures, none bearing on DFC or on any worst-case bound.
